title: Immune checkpoint TIM-3 regulates microglia and Alzheimer's disease
one_line: The authors show that the immune checkpoint receptor TIM-3 (HAVCR2), whose gene carries an Alzheimer's-associated polymorphism, is induced on aged/homeostatic microglia and restrains their phagocytic clearance of amyloid-beta, with microglia-specific deletion reducing plaque burden and improving cognition in 5xFAD mice.
key_claims: HAVCR2, encoding TIM-3, harbours a polymorphism associated with late-onset Alzheimer's disease, linking an immune checkpoint to AD genetics.
TIM-3 expression is upregulated on microglia with ageing and in the Alzheimer's disease brain, particularly in homeostatic rather than disease-associated microglial states.
Microglia-specific deletion of Havcr2 in the 5xFAD amyloidosis model increased microglial phagocytosis and uptake/clearance of amyloid-beta.
Havcr2 deletion reduced amyloid plaque burden and improved cognitive/behavioural performance in 5xFAD mice.

Loss of TIM-3 shifted microglial transcriptional programmes away from the homeostatic signature toward a phagocytic/disease-associated state, suggesting TIM-3 acts as a brake on protective microglial responses.
limitations: Findings rest on mouse amyloidosis models (5xFAD), which do not reproduce the full tau and neurodegenerative pathology of human Alzheimer's disease.
The human evidence is genetic association plus expression data, not a demonstration that the HAVCR2 variant alters microglial TIM-3 function in patients.
Whether blocking TIM-3 therapeutically (rather than genetic deletion from development) confers the same benefit, and at what disease stage, was not established.
Risks of removing an inhibitory checkpoint in the CNS — chronic inflammation, off-target immune activation, or effects on peripheral immunity — were not fully characterised.
open_questions: Does pharmacological anti-TIM-3 blockade in aged or established-pathology models reproduce the genetic deletion phenotype without inflammatory toxicity?
Do human carriers of the AD-associated HAVCR2 variant show altered microglial TIM-3 levels or amyloid clearance in vivo?
Which ligand–receptor interaction (e.g. phosphatidylserine or other TIM-3 ligands on damaged neurons/plaques) mediates the phagocytic brake?
Does TIM-3 loss affect tau pathology and neurodegeneration, not just amyloid plaque burden?
